lead: Numerical aperture, cutoff wavelength and cladding diameter decide whether a fiber behaves as a single-mode guide at the operating wavelength. All three are read from light leaving the fiber: a far-field pattern, a bend-loss trace, or an index profile. The same instruments travel to the field, where an installed cable is tested with a source and power meter, an OTDR, a visual fault locator, dispersion testers and a bit-error test. Only a few universities teach this measurement detail.
prereq: You need Unit 1 for numerical aperture and cutoff wavelength, and 5.4 for the measurement bench.

blocks.text: Cutoff wavelength is the wavelength above which the fiber carries only the fundamental mode. The bend, or transmission, method uses a 2 m length. Launch the broad-spectrum source into one length of fiber and record the trace straight, then with one loop, comparing the two traces of the same fiber. Record output power against wavelength for both. Below cutoff the fiber guides the fundamental mode and also a weakly confined higher-order mode (for example LP11); the bend strips the higher-order mode, so the looped trace loses power. Above cutoff that higher-order mode is no longer guided, only the well-confined fundamental remains, and the bend removes very little, so the gap closes. Cutoff is the wavelength where the looped trace sits a fixed amount below the straight one; a common criterion is 0.1 dB. The standard transmission method uses a loop of 60 mm radius. The 2 m measurement gives the fiber cutoff wavelength; a longer cabled length gives the cable cutoff, which is shorter. Bend sensitivity of the fundamental itself grows with wavelength because the mode field widens. The result depends on loop diameter and launch condition, so report both. Do not call the link's operating wavelength the cutoff wavelength.

Numerical aperture NA is the sine of the half-angle θ at which the far-field intensity falls to 5% of its peak: NA = sin θ. Use the 5% level, not the 50% half-power level. The index profile gives approximately the same value: NA = √(n1² − n2²), where n1 is the core index and n2 the cladding index. The far-field NA usually comes out a little larger because of launch and mode-excitation effects, so expect a small difference from the profile number. Measured in air, the acceptance half-angle θa equals θ.

Core diameter comes from a refracted near-field index profile. Cladding diameter comes from a video microscope or a grey-scale image; 125 μm is standard for single-mode and most multimode fiber. Calibrate the microscope scale before measuring. A wrong diameter changes connector and splice loss. Reflectance is R = 10 log₁₀(P_r/P_i), where P_r is reflected power and P_i is incident power; R is negative, for example −30 dB. Optical return loss is ORL = −10 log₁₀(P_r/P_i); it is positive, so the same joint has ORL = 30 dB.

In the field, an installed link is tested without cutting it. A source and power meter give end-to-end loss. An OTDR sends a pulse and plots backscatter against distance; the trace locates splice loss, connector loss, bend loss and a break. A visual fault locator injects visible red light to find a tight bend or a cracked connector. Chromatic dispersion and polarization-mode dispersion testers check high-bit-rate routes. A bit-error-rate test runs known data and counts errors. Measure loss at the operating wavelength. Compare results with the power budget in 5.2 and the attenuation measurement in 5.4.

figure.caption: Below cutoff the fiber still guides a weakly confined higher-order mode, and the loop strips it, so the looped trace drops away; near 1200 nm the gap reaches the 0.1 dB criterion.

spec.aria: Plot of relative output against wavelength: a flat straight-fiber trace at 0 dB and a looped-fiber trace that falls steeply below about 1200 nm because the bend strips a weakly confined higher-order mode.

examples.question: A step-index fiber has n1 = 1.46. In the far field the intensity falls to 5% of its peak at a half-angle of 12° from the axis. Find the numerical aperture, the acceptance angle in air and n2.
steps: Measured in air, the acceptance angle θa equals this far-field half-angle, so θa = 12°.
examples.check:
import math
n1 = 1.46
theta_deg = 12
NA = math.sin(math.radians(theta_deg))
n2 = math.sqrt(n1**2 - NA**2)
print(round(NA, 3))
print(round(float(theta_deg), 1))
print(round(n2, 3))

traps: Calling the operating wavelength the cutoff wavelength.
Using the 50% far-field half-angle instead of the 5% level.
Giving reflectance a positive sign and ORL a negative sign.
Reporting cutoff without loop diameter and launch condition.
Measuring cladding diameter from the core index profile, or skipping microscope calibration.

quiz.q: State the far-field definition of numerical aperture.
quiz.a: NA = sin θ, where θ is the half-angle at which intensity is 5% of its peak.

quiz.q: Why does the looped fiber trace fall below the straight trace below cutoff?
quiz.a: Below cutoff a weakly confined higher-order mode also propagates and the bend strips it; above cutoff that mode is no longer guided, only the well-confined fundamental remains, and the two traces meet.

quiz.q: A fiber has n1 = 1.45 and NA = 0.22. Find n2.
Reflected power is 1 μW and incident power is 1 mW. Find reflectance and ORL.
A cutoff report gives 1210 nm but no loop diameter. Why is the number incomplete?
quiz.a: Cutoff depends on bend radius and launch condition; without them the value cannot be reproduced or compared.

quiz.q: What is the standard cladding diameter, and which instrument measures it?
quiz.a: 125 μm; a video microscope or a grey-scale image.

beyond: Not for the exam. Field technicians carry OTDR modules that report splice loss and reflectance on one trace. PON installers use a visual fault locator and a power meter at the customer end. Factory benches use refracted near-field profilers to certify core diameter and index profile. Search for OTDR dead zone, bend-insensitive fiber and G.650 test methods if you meet these in a lab.
